Question 1
A DBMS is usually explained with the three-schema architecture. The external level contains different user views, the conceptual level is the complete logical schema, and the internal level describes files, pages and indexes. Mappings provide logical and physical data independence.

The query processor includes the DDL interpreter, SQL parser and semantic checker, DML compiler, cost-based optimizer and execution engine. It consults the system catalog for table, constraint and statistics information. The storage manager contains the file/index manager and buffer manager, which move pages between disk and memory. It also coordinates the authorization/integrity manager and transaction manager. Persistent storage includes data files, indexes, catalog and log.

For transactions, locking or MVCC provides isolation, the recovery manager uses WAL, checkpoints, redo and undo, and authorization and constraints protect valid data. When SQL arrives, it is parsed and checked, optimized into a physical plan, and executed. Operators request pages through the buffer manager while locks/versions and log records are maintained. Commit makes the work durable and the result is returned through the user's external view. Caching, indexes, optimization and controlled concurrency make this efficient.

Question 2
The hierarchical model organizes records as a tree with one parent per child. Path navigation is fast and integrity is simple for fixed one-to-many data, so it suits file systems and legacy IMS-style applications. It is rigid, duplicates data for many-to-many relationships and is difficult to reorganize.

The network model forms a graph using record types and set/pointer links. A record can have several parents, so many-to-many relationships and navigational performance are better than hierarchical. Its schema and procedural access paths are complex and create program-data dependence. It was used in telecom and legacy manufacturing systems.

The relational model uses tables, rows, columns, primary/foreign keys and declarative SQL. It supports normalization, constraints, ad-hoc queries and strong standards, making it suitable for banking, education and business systems. Complex joins can be costly and rich objects may require mapping.

The object-oriented model persists objects with identity, classes, methods, inheritance and complex values. It fits CAD, multimedia and scientific systems but has fewer standards, tools and trained users. Therefore fixed tree navigation favors hierarchical, graph-like legacy navigation favors network, ordinary transactional data favors relational, and behavior-rich complex objects favor object-oriented.

Question 3
SQL is a declarative relational language: users state the required result or change, while the DBMS chooses the execution plan. It covers schema definition, data change, retrieval, security and transaction control.

DDL defines database objects: CREATE TABLE Student(id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(80)); ALTER TABLE Student ADD email VARCHAR(120) UNIQUE; TRUNCATE removes all rows and DROP removes the object. DML changes rows, for example INSERT INTO Student VALUES(1,'Asha'), UPDATE Student SET name='Ashi' WHERE id=1, and DELETE FROM Student WHERE id=1. DQL usually refers to SELECT, such as SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM Employee WHERE active=true GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*)>5 ORDER BY department.

DCL controls privileges: GRANT SELECT ON Student TO lecturer_role and REVOKE UPDATE ON Student FROM assistant_role. TCL manages a unit of work with BEGIN, SAVEPOINT s1, COMMIT and ROLLBACK [TO s1]. A typical lifecycle is CREATE constrained tables, GRANT suitable rights, start a transaction, perform INSERT/UPDATE and SELECT, then COMMIT if all operations succeed or ROLLBACK on error. Thus SQL supports structure, integrity, querying, updates, security and reliable transactions.

Question 4
A join combines rows from two relation sources according to an ON predicate, normally matching a foreign key with a primary key. For Employee(employee_id,name,dept_id,manager_id) and Department(dept_id,dept_name), INNER JOIN returns only matches: SELECT e.name,d.dept_name FROM Employee e INNER JOIN Department d ON e.dept_id=d.dept_id.

LEFT JOIN keeps every Employee and places NULL in department columns when there is no match. RIGHT JOIN keeps every Department, including departments without employees. FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides. Filters on the optional table usually belong in ON; putting them in WHERE can remove NULL-extended rows and turn an outer join effectively into an inner join.

CROSS JOIN returns every employee-department combination and needs no predicate, so its size is m*n. A SELF JOIN aliases one table twice, for example SELECT e.name,m.name AS manager FROM Employee e LEFT JOIN Employee m ON e.manager_id=m.employee_id. Equi and non-equi predicates may be used. One-to-many matches legitimately repeat the parent row, while a missing or incomplete predicate produces an accidental Cartesian product. Join type is chosen according to whether unmatched rows must be retained.

The external, conceptual and internal levels separate user views, the logical database and physical files. Their mappings give data independence, so storage changes need not change applications.

SQL first goes to the query processor. The parser checks syntax and names, the compiler translates it, the optimizer chooses scans, indexes and join order, and the execution engine runs the plan. DDL is recorded in the catalog. The storage manager has file, index and buffer managers and accesses data files, indexes and metadata. Transaction services include concurrency control, recovery, authorization and integrity checking.

A SELECT is parsed using catalog metadata, optimized, then its operators request pages from the buffer pool. The transaction manager obtains locks or an MVCC snapshot. Updates are logged before changed pages reach disk. COMMIT and recovery give durability and atomicity. I explained the flow, although I did not discuss every internal catalog component separately.

Question 2
Hierarchical databases are trees: one parent may have many children but a child normally has one parent. They are fast for known paths and suit organization charts or legacy records, but structural change and many-to-many data are awkward.

Network databases use records connected as a graph and allow several parents. They model many-to-many links and navigate efficiently, but pointer-based design and queries are complicated. Relational databases use tables and keys with SQL. They are simple, normalized, standardized and flexible for business applications; many joins and object mapping can add cost.

Object-oriented databases store objects, object identity, inheritance and methods. They suit engineering, multimedia and complex data, but have less standard query support and a smaller ecosystem. Model choice depends on relationship shape, access pattern, complexity and required standards. I gave fewer concrete network applications.

Question 3
SQL is declarative because we specify what data is required rather than the file-access algorithm. It is based on relational tables and is used by applications and administrators.

DDL includes CREATE, ALTER, TRUNCATE and DROP for schemas and constraints. Example: CREATE TABLE Course(code VARCHAR(8) PRIMARY KEY,title TEXT). DML includes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. DQL is SELECT with WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY. DCL uses GRANT and REVOKE to assign or remove privileges. TCL uses BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT for transactions.

An administrator creates a table and grants access. An application begins a transaction, inserts an enrolment, updates a seat count, queries the result and commits; it rolls back if either change fails. I did not explain vendor differences around whether SELECT is classified separately as DQL.

Question 4
Joins retrieve related columns by comparing keys in an ON condition. INNER JOIN Employee to Department on dept_id returns only employees whose department exists.

LEFT OUTER JOIN returns all employees plus matching department data, using NULL for an unmatched department. RIGHT JOIN keeps all departments, and FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both tables. CROSS JOIN produces all possible row pairs. SELF JOIN uses aliases of the same table, such as Employee e joined to Employee m on e.manager_id=m.employee_id.

An ON predicate is important to prevent an unwanted Cartesian product. Also, a WHERE condition on the nullable side of an outer join can remove its unmatched rows. I explained the result differences, although I gave complete SQL only for INNER and SELF joins.
